title: The elephant that would not charge
hookLine: Kabir sings of being bound and thrown before an elephant that bowed instead (Gond, Kabir, ang 870)

cards: His arms are tied. He's been bundled up like a sack and thrown down on the ground. Across the yard, a man sits high on an elephant's neck with a goad in his hand, and an official is shouting at him to drive it forward.
The elephant is huge. The man on the ground is a weaver. Everyone watching knows how this is supposed to end.
Except it doesn't. The one who tells us so is the man in the bundle: Kabir sings it himself, in a hymn in Raag Gond.

teach.b: Here's how the hymn tells it. They bound his arms and threw him down like a lump. The driver, in anger, struck the elephant on the head.
But the elephant turned and ran, crying out, as Kabir hears it, I am a sacrifice to this form of the Lord.

teach.h: DRIVE IT ON, SHOUTS THE JUDGE.
teach.b: The official, whom the hymn calls the qazi, the judge, shouts at the driver: drive it on, or I'll cut you down. The elephant won't move. The hymn says it stands still in meditation, because the Lord lives in its heart.

teach.h: WHAT WRONG HAS THIS SAINT DONE?
teach.b: Then Kabir asks the question at the center: what wrong has this saint done, that you tied him in a bundle and gave him to the elephant? And the elephant lifts the bundle again and again, and bows to it.
The judge, Kabir says, was in the dark and didn't see. Sikhs hold this hymn in more than one way.
Some take it just as it's sung, a wonder that really happened to Kabir.
Others hear the elephant as a picture too: the huge, angry force of the world, which, faced with someone whose heart rests in the Lord, can't find its target.
Both readings end at the hymn's last line: Kabir says the Lord of the world is mine, and the devotee's life rests in the fourth state. Kabir doesn't fight, and he doesn't curse the judge.
He stays, and the elephant bowed.

how: Sikhs sing Kabir's Gond hymn of the elephant in kirtan, and katha tellers retell it as a story of a devotee's steadiness before power.

o: a judge, the official in Kabir's hymn
a holy man who blessed the elephant
the driver who sat on the elephant's neck

games.q: the elephant that would not charge — tap the pairs.
p: struck the elephant on the head
was in the dark and didn't see

s: this story comes only from later tellers, not from Kabir
Kabir sings it himself, in a hymn in Raag Gond.
in the hymn, Kabir fights back against the driver
he doesn't fight or curse. he asks what wrong the saint has done.
the hymn says the elephant bowed to the bundle
it lifted the bundle again and again, and bowed.

games.q: you're the elephant. the driver strikes your head and the judge is shouting. on the ground in front of you, a man lies bound in a bundle. what do you do?
o: charge, as you were driven to.
turn away, then lift the bundle and bow.
games.why: in Kabir's hymn the elephant runs, won't be driven, and then lifts the bundle again and again and bows to it.

practice: Bring to mind one thing ahead of you that feels like an elephant, a hard conversation, a test, a bill, a diagnosis, a deadline, and let it stand there full size, without shrinking it and without running.
Breathe slowly in its presence, feet on the ground, as steady as the man in the bundle. If you pray, you can rest one Waheguru on each slow breath.

wordCard.voice: Qazi. The judge in Kabir's hymn, who ordered the elephant driven at him, and watched the elephant turn and bow instead.

carryVoice: Your line: the elephant bowed. The man in the bundle didn't run. See you tomorrow.
